newsitem.title: UK: Eastern Europe waking up to convertible bonds.
newsitem.headline: Eastern Europe waking up to convertible bonds.

text.p: Polish companies will issue their first convertible bonds in the coming months and others in the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Russia could follow, bankers said on Thursday.
Record highs on many of the region's stock markets have boosted demand for equity-related paper, and convertible bonds provide a less risky way of gaining exposure.

"Convertible bonds are an ideal product for fast-developing markets and have been used in Asia and South Africa," said David Meacher, capital markets manager at Robert Fleming. "It is a natural progression for eastern Europe to start issuing them."
Convertible bonds, which pay a relatively low coupon, give investors the option to swap their bond holdings into shares.
The conversion price is pre-set at a premium to the company's market level at the time of pricing. If the conversion option is not exercised, the issue is redeemed at par.
"Convertibles give investors a current running yield but the equity element provides a kicker if the stock market takes off," Richard Roberts, assistant director at WestMerchant said.
The conversion premium is a function of both how the wider stock market performs and of the company's own prospects.
"The premium on eastern European convertibles will range between a minimum of 10 percent to up to around 30 percent for Russian high volatility stocks," said Meacher at Flemings.
In May 1996, computer maker Optimus SA issued a $30 million convertible private placement. Launched via Merrill Lynch, the paper was bought by just a handful of investors.
The deal was launched at a 20 percent premium for a converson price of 38.76 zlotys per share. Optimus was trading at 61 zlotys on Thursday.
Uncertainty about the direction of interest rates will also boost demand for convertibles, dealers said.
"It is a good environment for convertible bonds generally," said Crispin Osborne, director at Credit Suisse First Boston.

"There are historically low interest rates and historically high equity markets, and high levels of redemptions, prompting substantial demand for securities that provide downside protection," he said.
"Transactions may emerge from Poland, Hungary the Czech Republic and Russia in 1997," he said.
POLISH DEALS IN THE PIPELINE
Two Polish companies and one Polish bank have already announced plans for public convertible bonds.
Steelmaker Stalexport plans to issue a $50 million five- to seven-year convertible bond with a call after three years via Robert Fleming in March, Meacher said.
Polish Bank Przemyslowo-Handlowy (BPH) shareholders this week approved a convertible for up to $100 million with a maturity of up to five years via CSFB.
Polish trading and industrial conglomorate Elektrim also plans a deal, which could be for $100 million, dealers said.
"Stalexport will be the first standard Euroconvertible offering from the region to a wide range of investors, and it will be the first to be listed," said Meacher.
Hungary was the region's star performer in 1996, with its stock market rising 170 percent in local currency terms, and Poland followed with nearly 90 percent gains.
Improved investor confidence in the region, as well as increased familiarity with its companies means investors are now prepared to commit more funds.
But before launching the first public Euroconvertible bond in any country, a host of regulatory obstacles must be overcome.
"Laws are now just about adequate in Poland. But whoever does the first deal in another country will have a lot of work to do," said Meacher.
The list of potential candidates is limited because companies need a market capitalisation of at least $100 million to issue a convertible bond, dealers said
"Utilities, banks and engineering and agricultural companies are all looking, but there are only about 30 possible public entities who could launch deals," said Roberts at WestMerchant.
